content: The Credit Risk dataset covers 1,928,413 card transactions across roughly 5,000 cardholders and 4,000 cards, recorded between June 1, 2024 and May 31, 2026 (24 months).

Confirmed fraud is rare: only 2,197 of 1,928,413 transactions are flagged fraud (0.114% by count). Always reason about fraud in basis points, not whole percentages, and never expect fraud to dominate transaction-level aggregates.
The transactions table keys on card_id and merchant_id, not customer_id. To analyze fraud by customer segment, join transactions → cards → customers on card_id then customer_id.

Across 382 fraud episodes, ₹6.15 crore was attempted, ₹4.18 crore (68%) was prevented by real-time blocking, and ₹1.97 crore (32%) was actually lost. 'Amount prevented' vs 'amount lost' is the headline effectiveness metric for the fraud program.

Fraud typology mix by episode: CNP international e-commerce is largest at 98 episodes (26%), followed by OTP social-engineering account takeover (65, 17%), card testing (60, 16%), skimming/clone (50, 13%), and lost/stolen (40, 10%). Mule cycling, merchant collusion, and subscription drain make up the tail.

Card-not-present (CNP) international e-commerce is both the most common and the highest-loss typology, which is typical: no chip/PIN present, cross-border rules are weaker, and recovery is hardest once funds leave the country.

Card-testing (BIN attack) episodes show as a rapid burst of small-value authorizations on a card within minutes, as fraudsters validate stolen card numbers before a large purchase. Velocity and small-amount-cluster rules are the primary defense.

OTP social-engineering account takeover (ATO) is the second-largest typology: the customer is tricked into sharing an OTP, so the transaction passes 3DS authentication. Auth success does not imply a genuine transaction — pair auth_method with behavioral risk signals.

Alert quality is the core operational tension: of 32,857 alerts, 29,442 were dispositioned false positive and only 1,519 true positive — a precision of about 4.9% among resolved alerts (roughly 19 false alerts per real fraud). 1,896 remain unresolved.

Low alert precision is expected in fraud operations because misses are far costlier than false alarms, so rules are tuned for recall. The real cost of a high false-positive rate is customer friction (good transactions declined) and analyst workload, not direct loss.

Analyst average handle time is about 793 seconds (~13 minutes) per alert, with 1,422 alerts breaching their SLA target. Handle time and SLA-breach rate are the key queue-health metrics; segment them by shift (DAY/EVENING/NIGHT) to find staffing gaps.

Liability outcomes on resolved fraud cases: 1,143 zero-liability (72%), 379 limited-liability (24%), and 72 customer-liable (4.5%). Zero-liability dominates because most genuine victims report quickly.

Liability follows RBI's limited-liability framework (circular dated 6 July 2017): a customer bears zero liability when unauthorized use is reported within 3 working days, and limited liability for delays of 4–7 working days. The reporting_delay_bucket field maps directly to this rule.

A fraud episode groups multiple fraudulent transactions on the same compromise into one incident. Count episodes (not individual transactions) when measuring fraud incidents, typologies, and detection time; count transactions only for amount math.

Detection source matters for benchmarking: system real-time catches drive 'amount prevented', while customer-reported and batch detections usually correlate with higher 'amount lost' because the fraud completed before a block. Compare time_to_detect across detection_source values.

Industry benchmark: global card fraud runs roughly 6–7 basis points of transaction value (Nilson Report). This dataset's 0.114% fraud-by-count is in a realistic range for an Indian issuer once weighted by amount, where intl CNP skews loss higher than count.

Industry benchmark: well-run card-fraud systems target alert precision in the 5–20% range and recall (fraud-caught) above 80%; chasing higher precision usually sacrifices catch rate. Use this to frame whether the current 4.9% precision needs rule tuning.

A clean fraud-detection funnel for this data is: transaction → risk-scored → alert raised → analyst decision → disposition (true/false positive) → blocking action → case resolution. Each stage narrows; conversion between stages reveals where loss leaks through.

When computing fraud-loss rates, use amount_lost_inr from fraud_episodes as the numerator and total approved purchase value as the denominator. Do not divide loss by transaction count — that mixes value and volume.

Customer segments (Classic, Preferred, Imperia) carry different risk and spend profiles; premium tiers see more international and high-ticket spend, so absolute fraud exposure can be higher even when their fraud rate is similar. Always segment fraud metrics by customer tier before drawing conclusions.
